summary: Rogers and Pingali compile a sequential Id-like program together with a data decomposition into per-process C code for the Intel iPSC/2, using run-time resolution as a correct fallback and compile-time resolution where ownership can be analyzed. Vectorization, pipelining and accumulation of messages are added, and the Gauss-Seidel measurements show the best variant at about three quarters of the speed of handwritten code, while SIMPLE speeds up to 32 processors.
why_read: It is a clear early account of owner-driven process decomposition with a correct fallback, and of the message optimizations needed to make such generated code usable.
main_contribution: A data-driven compilation method with run-time and compile-time resolution, plus vectorization, pipelining and accumulation of messages for distributed-memory code.
main_limitation: Compile-time resolution cannot help with complex or irregular data structures whose references are not analyzable, and the generated code remains slower than handwritten code.
evaluation_method: Timings of code variants on iPSC/2 compared with handwritten code for Gauss-Seidel, and SIMPLE speedup compared with a modeled handwritten program.
benchmarks: Gauss-Seidel on a 128x128 grid, iPSC/2, 4 to 32 processors
SIMPLE hydrodynamics benchmark on a 64x64 grid, iPSC/2, 1 to 32 processors
